questions.question: What does append() do in Go, and why must you assign its result?
questions.title: Ppend() Do In Go, And Why Must
questions.direct_answer: append returns a possibly-new header: in place if capacity remains, reallocated if not. The header may change, so the caller must reassign: s = append(s, x).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Append And Growth beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: append returns a possibly-new header: in place if capacity remains, reallocated if not. The header may change, so.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Append takes a slice and one or more values, and returns a slice — that return is the contract. Two things can happen inside. If the backing array has spare capacity, the value is written into the next slot and the same header (with len bumped) comes back — no allocation. If the slice is at capacity, append allocates a bigger array, copies everything over, and returns a header pointing at the new storage.

Because you can't know from the call site which happened, the only safe pattern is reassignment. `s = append(s, x)` works in both cases. Skipping the assignment is a real bug: when growth occurred, the caller keeps the old header — pointing at the old array — and the appended element is invisible. The classic shape is appending in a helper and losing the growth in the caller.

The corollary: append never mutates the header you passed; it returns the up-to-date one. The elements may be shared — in-place writes are visible to aliases — but the header itself is only ever returned, never modified in place.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[append s x] --> C{len < cap?}
    C -->|yes| IN[write in place — aliases see it]
    C -->|no len == cap| ALLOC[allocate ~2x array]
    ALLOC --> COPY[copy elements]
    COPY --> FORK[new storage — old aliases fork]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why is reassignment the only safe pattern? Because the two modes are indistinguishable from the call site:

```go
s := make([]int, 0, 4)
s = append(s, 1)  // in-place mode (cap 4 spare)
s = append(s, 2)  // in-place mode
newS := append(s, 3)  // still in-place, but imagine this was at cap
```

In the at-cap case, the old `s` and the returned slice are two different windows onto two different arrays. The runtime didn't update `s`'s header — it can't, the header lives in your variable. So append's return value is the new truth, and the old variable is stale the moment capacity was exceeded.

This is the mechanism behind Go's most-found code review comment (`s = append(s, ...)` missing). The go vet tool has never flagged it because both modes are legal Go — it's a semantic stale-reference bug, invisible to static checks, which is why the idiom must be muscle memory.

questions.question: Does append always allocate new memory?
questions.title: Does Append Always Allocate New Memory
questions.direct_answer: No — below capacity it writes in place into the existing array, visible to every alias. Only at len == cap does it allocate, copy, and fork.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Append And Growth.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: No — below capacity it writes in place into the existing array, visible to every alias.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
It depends entirely on where the length sits relative to capacity, and the distinction has real correctness consequences — not just performance ones.

Spare capacity: append writes the element into the next slot of the existing backing array. No allocation, no copy — and every other slice sharing that array sees the write. This is the fastest path, and it's the one that makes sub-slice-then-append change the original slice, the classic aliasing surprise.

At capacity: append allocates a new array sized for growth, copies the old elements in, appends the new one, and returns the new header. Slices still viewing the old array don't see any of this — they've permanently forked.

So the honest phrasing is 'may allocate'. Any code whose correctness depends on either branch — sharing preserved, or sharing severed — needs to control capacity deliberately rather than rely on append's choice.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[append s x] --> C{len < cap?}
    C -->|yes| IN[write in place — aliases see it]
    C -->|no len == cap| ALLOC[allocate ~2x array]
    ALLOC --> COPY[copy elements]
    COPY --> FORK[new storage — old aliases fork]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two modes, traced against the same start:

```go
// Mode A: spare capacity — in-place
a := make([]int, 2, 4)   // len 2, cap 4 — two spare slots
b := append(a, 9)       // writes a's array[2] — shared
b[0] = 100
fmt.Println(a[0])       // 100 — a sees it, same array

// Mode B: at capacity — fork
c := []int{1, 2}        // len 2, cap 2 — no spare
d := append(c, 9)       // allocates new array, copies
d[0] = 100
fmt.Println(c[0])       // 1 — c points at the old array
```

Same operation, opposite sharing outcomes — the only variable was capacity. This is why append-heavy APIs document their aliasing behavior: callers who pass a sub-slice and later read the original need to know which mode they'll get.

The performance angle is real too — pre-sizing with `make([]T, 0, n)` pins every append to mode A, turning an O(n²) grow-copy chain into O(n) total — but it's the correctness angle that bites in code review.

questions.question: How can you make append allocation-free when the final size is known?
questions.title: Can You Make Append Allocation-free When The
questions.direct_answer: make([]T, 0, n) up front — every append then writes in place within capacity. One allocation instead of the grow-copy chain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Append And Growth.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: make([]T, 0, n) up front — every append then writes in place within capacity. One allocation instead of.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you know how many elements you'll end up with — a loop over a known input, a transformation with 1:1 output — you can pre-allocate the destination with capacity and let append only ever take its in-place path.

```go
out := make([]string, 0, len(input))
for _, v := range input {
    out = append(out, transform(v))
}
```

Each append writes into the next spare slot — no reallocation, no copies of the growing prefix, no transient garbage arrays. The whole build is one allocation of len(input) slots and n direct stores.

The pattern applies anywhere the bound is knowable: a filter that keeps at most len(input) items, a batch of results sized by request, a buffer for a read whose maximum size is documented. Where the size is only estimated, the capacity hint still amortizes growth even if it misses.

This is the standard-libraray idiom too — bytes.Buffer grows similarly behind the scenes, and slices pre-sized in hot paths are one of the easiest real performance wins in Go.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[append s x] --> C{len < cap?}
    C -->|yes| IN[write in place — aliases see it]
    C -->|no len == cap| ALLOC[allocate ~2x array]
    ALLOC --> COPY[copy elements]
    COPY --> FORK[new storage — old aliases fork]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why is this such a win? Compare the allocation behavior:

Growth mode (no pre-size): appending 1000 elements to a zero-cap slice allocates and copies at roughly every doubling — the array moves through cap 1, 2, 4, 8 ... 1024, copying the prefix each time. Total element copies: about 2000 for 1000 appends. Plus each abandoned array is garbage for the GC to collect.

Pre-sized mode: `make([]T, 0, 1000)` allocates once, appends are pointer-bumps, total copies zero. Same final slice, radically different work.

That's the amortized-analysis story from dynamic arrays, applied by hand. The runtime's doubling keeps append O(1) average even without pre-sizing — you never need this for correctness — but the constant factors differ by orders of magnitude in hot loops. Profile first, but when a loop's shape makes the final size knowable, this is the cheapest optimization in the language.

questions.question: Why is append(s, x) without assignment a classic Go bug?
questions.title: Is Append(s, X) Without Assignment A Classic
questions.direct_answer: When growth occurs, the new header lives only in the return value. The original s still points at the old array — the appended element is lost to the caller.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Append And Growth.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: When growth occurs, the new header lives only in the return value.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The bug hides because it's intermittent: append sometimes works without assignment. While capacity remains, the returned header equals the original — same pointer, same array — so `append(s, x)` without capturing the result still leaves the element visible through s. The code passes its tests.

Then an input one element longer arrives, capacity is exceeded, append allocates a new array, and the element goes into the copy that's returned — which is discarded. The caller's s still views the old array. No error, no panic: the element just doesn't exist as far as any reader of s can tell.

That silence is what makes it pernicious. Go's compiler won't flag it — the call is legal — and the failure only appears under the capacity-exceeded branch. The guard is purely idiomatic: always write `s = append(s, x)`, even when you're sure capacity remains, because 'sure' is what the bug waits for.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[append s x] --> C{len < cap?}
    C -->|yes| IN[write in place — aliases see it]
    C -->|no len == cap| ALLOC[allocate ~2x array]
    ALLOC --> COPY[copy elements]
    COPY --> FORK[new storage — old aliases fork]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two-timeline trace makes the failure concrete:

```go
func addTo(data []int, items ...int) {
    for _, it := range items {
        data = append(data, it)  // correct: reassigns
    }
    _ = data  // if this were the bug version, data's growth would be local-only
}

// the bug shape:
s := make([]int, 0, 2)
append(s, 1)   // fits in cap — works, s sees 1 through... nothing
append(s, 2)   // fits — s would see [1 2] if reassigned
append(s, 3)   // cap exceeded — allocates, but the header is DISCARDED
fmt.Println(len(s))  // 0 — none of it was ever captured
```

The prints show the whole mechanism: append always returns the current truth, and the caller's variable only updates by assignment. The runtime never reaches back into your variable — that's what passing by value means for the header.

This is why linters like golangci-lint grew an `appendAssign` check — the bug is invisible to the compiler, common in quick code, and only detectable by recognizing the discarded-result shape. Know the idiom before you need the linter.

questions.question: What is the growth factor of Go slices?
questions.title: Growth Factor Of Go Slices
questions.direct_answer: Roughly doubling for small slices — a slice at cap 3 grows to 6, then 12. Growth tapers for very large slices to avoid over-allocating.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Append And Growth.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Roughly doubling for small slices — a slice at cap 3 grows to 6, then 12.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For small slices, Go grows capacity by about 2x each time capacity is exceeded. A slice created from a 3-element literal grows to 6 when you append a fourth, then to 12, then 24 — you can watch it with cap prints. This is the standard dynamic-array strategy: doubling gives amortized O(1) appends, meaning n appends cost about 2n element-copies total instead of the O(n²) of one-at-a-time growth.

For large slices, the factor shrinks. Doubling a 2GB slice means allocating 4GB — most programs would rather the runtime grow more gently toward 1.25x-ish at those sizes. The exact transition points are runtime-version-specific, which is why the honest interview answer is 'about 2x for small, tapering for large, and an implementation detail you should never depend on.'

Depend on the amortized bound — the language guarantees that — not on any specific capacity sequence. Code that requires cap to be an exact value after growth should allocate its own arrays.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[append s x] --> C{len < cap?}
    C -->|yes| IN[write in place — aliases see it]
    C -->|no len == cap| ALLOC[allocate ~2x array]
    ALLOC --> COPY[copy elements]
    COPY --> FORK[new storage — old aliases fork]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Watching the growth live:

```go
s := []int{1}          // cap 1
s = append(s, 2)       // 1→2
s = append(s, 3)       // 2→4
s = append(s, 4)
s = append(s, 5)       // 4→8
for len(s) <= 20 {
    s = append(s, 0)
}
fmt.Println(cap(s))     // powers of two: 32 (on this run)
```

Each print shows the runtime's next tier. The sequence is stable for small sizes, which is why tutorials show it — but the runtime reserves the right to change the schedule (and has, across versions), so the sequence is an observation, not a contract.

The amortized bound is the contract: append is O(1) average, with occasional O(n) copies when the tier boundary is crossed. Pre-sizing (the earlier question) doesn't change the bound — it just deletes the copies for a known n. For unknown n, doubling is mathematically the least-copy schedule for growth-by-append, which is why every major dynamic array (Go slices, C++ vector, Python list, Java ArrayList) uses it.
